proposed.demonstrated_gap: Durable Python steps and long waits with the smallest footprint among step-checkpointing engines. The README says DBOS 'is entirely contained in this open-source library, there's no additional infrastructure' beyond Postgres. There is no server or worker fleet as with Temporal, and a systemd --user unit (the winner) can supervise the process. It meets the layer's long-waits trigger directly: durable sleep 'stores its wakeup time in Postgres so the workflow sleeps through any interruption or restart', and resume restarts a workflow 'from its last completed step'. The new rewind (3.1.0, 2026-09-24) re-executes from a chosen step while keeping the workflow ID, which the docs call 'useful when the ID is an idempotency key derived from an order or request ID'; that bears on open gap 2 (broker order effects). Visible history is local through dbos workflow list and dbos workflow steps, with cancel and resume from the CLI. The 2026-09-26 not_adopted reason still holds in the docs: cancellation 'preempts its execution (interrupting it at the beginning of its next step)', and only steps marked preemptible cancel immediately. But the retained Temporal port needs the same kind of adapter to stop a running subprocess, so that reason alone does not separate DBOS from the kept challenger. 3.0.0 (2026-09-16) is a major version with schema changes. proposed.demonstrated_gap: A Postgres-only durable task layer whose documented semantics address worker-host loss and long waits with no service beyond Postgres. The concepts page says that if a worker crashes or stalls before its lease expires, the task 'becomes available for another worker to pick up'. That covers any worker on any host sharing the database (open gap 1 for worker hosts; Dagu's #2805 is open). Completed steps are persisted and 'will never execute again'. Tasks 'can run for seconds, days, or years' and can suspend to sleep or wait for an event, then resume from the last checkpoint. The spawn-time policies maxDuration and maxDelay cancel overlong or stalled tasks. It has a Python SDK and uvx absurdctl to initialise, inspect and retry tasks. The same page names the costs a trial must test: 'brief overlapping execution is possible', and running tasks 'detect cancellation at the next checkpoint write or heartbeat call'. Neither is OS-level bounding of a subprocess tree. Maintenance is lower but not stale: the latest default-branch commit and release 0.5.0 are both from 2026-08-04. It is the previous sweep's compare-only survivor and stays compare-only as a thinner Postgres-only alternative to DBOS.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn:
Run the same fixture port as the DBOS entry, using the Python SDK and absurdctl against one Postgres. Put workers on the WSL2 workstation and a Mac, with the work directory shared or carried as a step result. Add the cases its concepts page flags: an expired-lease worker still running (no duplicate completed.json), an effect committed before its checkpoint persists, and cancellation of a blocked subprocess (zero descendants within the bound).
Passing all of them within 150 s with a footprint no larger than DBOS makes it a targeted Postgres-only option. Duplicate effects, unbounded subprocesses, or no default-branch commit by 2026-11-02 (stale under the 90-day rule) make it not_adopted.

This means brief overlapping execution is possible'; 'Running tasks detect cancellation at the next checkpoint write or heartbeat call'; maxDuration and maxDelay; 'Code outside steps may execute multiple times across retries'

WINNER HEALTH

WINNER STANDING
- Dagu's crash-recovery standing is unproven either way. The retained SIGKILL comparison ran under unequal configurations: Temporal had a tuned 5 s heartbeat, while Dagu ran without a scheduler, or with default liveness (90 s stale threshold, 3 checks at 45 s) that fits its ~182 s. The Dagu targeted trial settles it.
- Dagu's standing on graceful stop, retry, checkpoint reuse and native process-tree stop is evidence-based (WSL2 and macOS receipts).
- systemd's per-host bounded-tree standing is evidence-based: real paper-lane runs use systemd-run --user with KillMode=control-group and RuntimeMaxSec (mover-coverage-asof/README.md:44-46).
- Neither winner has host-loss evidence.

LAYER INPUT IS STALE AGAINST origin/main 703b2bd7
- Dagu macos-arm64 'untested' is contradicted by job-recovery/receipt-macos.json (Darwin 25.5.0 arm64, dagu 2.16.6, passed, 2026-09-20).
- Open gap 3 is stale: gap-wave2 2-real-workflow-scheduled-recovered.json is 'settled'. A real maintenance workflow with a model triage step was scheduled, stopped with dagu stop and retried under Dagu 2.16.6.

- Open gap 2 has advanced: 1-provider-cancel-broker-exactly-once.json shows dagu stop ended an in-flight codex exec tree within 150 ms. Provider-side cancellation and billing are unverified, and the broker arm was deferred. hosting.json:504 says engine adoption cannot create exactly-once broker effects.
- Cross-host arms need a shared work directory or a carried checkpoint payload, because fixture.py writes its state into a local work argument.

PRIOR REFUTATION RE-CHECK
- Restate's 2026-09-26 refutation came only from the GPT-6 fit vote's BSL license veto; the Claude fit vote kept it. It is re-proposed on merit.

STAR SCAN AND SEEDED CANDIDATES

- Seeded candidates: none.

NOT PROPOSED, NOT REFUTED

  - Retained evidence: 3.8.6 passed stop, retry and checkpoint reuse and stops step processes natively. It failed SIGKILL only because zombie-flow detection was not configured.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Open gap: recovery is not_established for PostgreSQL and no backup/independent-host restore acceptance exists. The in-winner tools close the basic gap first and bound pgBackRest's role. PG 18 docs 25.1 say pg_dump 'is also the only method that will work when transferring a database to a different machine architecture', and that file-level backups and continuous archiving are 'extremely server-version-specific'. WSL x86_64 to Mac arm64 restore is therefore logical only: pg_dump/pg_restore carried by the retained Restic. Over the in-winner physical path (pg_basebackup --incremental, pg_combinebackup, pg_verifybackup, a hand-written archive_command), pgBackRest adds a maintained same-architecture PITR pipeline. PG 25.3 says pg_dump 'cannot be used as part of a continuous-archiving solution' and that archive commands 'should generally be designed to refuse to overwrite any pre-existing archive file'. pgBackRest's WAL push de-duplicates identical segments and 'otherwise an error is raised'. Every file is checksummed and 'rechecked during a restore or verify', and 2.59.0 added backup.info checks to verify. 2.59.2 (2026-09-27) already supports PG 19beta4. No PITR/RPO requirement is defined, so this stays a comparison, not a trial.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Run only after a PITR or RPO requirement is defined. Hold one frozen acceptance: the fixture's ledger records compared byte-for-byte after restore (ID, timestamps, status, revision, history count). The feasible host pairs are fixed. The WSL fixture (the only x86_64 host) supports a same-host PITR restore into a fresh data directory. Its independent-host restore can only be logical, pg_dump -Fc plus the retained Restic 0.19.1 to an M5 Pro Mac (PG docs 25.1). The only same-architecture independent pair for a physical or PITR restore is the two arm64 Macs (24 GB and 64 GB). On macOS, pgBackRest is CI smoke-tested only (test-bsd.yml on macos-26) and ships no release binaries, so its Mac install route must be established first. Arms: (a) in-winner logical, pg_dump/pg_restore plus Restic; (b) in-winner physical, basic_archive or archive_command, pg_basebackup --incremental with summarize_wal, pg_combinebackup, pg_verifybackup, and recovery_target_time set just before a destructive migration; (c) pgBackRest 2.59.x with a local posix repo: stanza-create, check, full plus incremental backup, verify, restore --type=time to the same target. Plant a corrupted WAL segment and a duplicate archive push with different content. Measure restore correctness, recovery point reached against target, restore wall time, operator steps and config lines, detection of the planted faults, disk footprint and clean removal. pgBackRest wins only if (c) matches (b) on correctness and beats it on fault detection or operator steps. Otherwise the gap closes inside the winner. WAL-G v3.0.9 (Linux-only release binaries) and Barman 3.20.0 are same-class fallbacks only if (c) fails.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Open gap: 'Migration reversal proves schema reversal only, not user-data recovery or production-safe rollback.' The fixture migrates with Alembic (alembic.ini, migrations/versions/0001_run_ledger.py) and reverses by downgrade script. pgroll serves 'multiple schema versions simultaneously' through views over the physical tables. It can roll back 'at any point during a migration' while old clients keep working. That closes production-safe rollback for in-flight migrations only. After completion it recovers no user data, which stays with backups. It would also replace Alembic authoring with pgroll operation files. It matters only once a hosted or multi-client deployment must keep serving during schema changes, and none is defined. Platform: README says 'Works with Postgres 14.0 or later', and CI tests 14.8 through 18.0 plus latest. Maintenance fact: only 2 default-branch commits since 2026-07-01 (newest 2026-09-08) and about one release per quarter (v0.16.1 2026-02-17, v0.16.2 2026-05-12, v0.16.3 2026-09-08). Low activity, not stale.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Run after a hosted or multi-client requirement is defined. On the fixture at PostgreSQL 18.6, apply one breaking change to run_ledger (a column rename or split) while a load generator writes through the FastAPI API. Arm A: Alembic upgrade, then downgrade. Arm B: pgroll 0.16.x start, then rollback, and separately start then complete. Measure failed API requests during the migration window, rows written during that window that survive rollback or downgrade, migration and rollback wall time, and authoring cost (Alembic Python against pgroll operations). Also check whether the SQLAlchemy client can target the versioned schema without code changes. Adopt pgroll only if B shows zero failed requests and full preservation of in-window writes where A fails or loses them.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: This is open gap 5. The recorded off-host restore keeps ciphertext and password delivery under one GitHub account. Its README says it 'cannot qualify ... loss of the GitHub account, long-term retention, lost-password recovery, ... or independence from GitHub as the common hosting and secret-management provider' (blueprints/convergence-practice/offhost-restore/README.md lines 132-135). A grep of adoption, docs, blueprints and catalogs on origin/main 703b2bd7 finds no restic copy, --from-repo or rest-server recipe. So the selected recipes record no second independent repository and no deletion protection. Native restic already covers the location and password halves: restic copy into a second repository created with init --from-repo --copy-chunker-params, and restic key add with a password delivered offline. rest-server therefore does not uniquely close gap 5. What it adds is --append-only on an independent host, which its README says 'prevents an attacker from wiping your server backups when access is gained to the server being backed up'. It also verifies uploads by default (a --no-verify-upload flag exists to turn that off). rclone serve restic --append-only is the equivalent comparison arm. rest-server already survived 2026-09-26 as keep_but_compare in the trading observability-hosting layer. This is its first assessment for this layer, and upstream has not changed since (still v0.14.0). No independent target host is explicitly adopted today (macos-arm64 is drafted_not_accepted), so no trial is feasible now.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: The trial starts once an independent target host is explicitly adopted. (1) Run restic init --from-repo --copy-chunker-params, then restic copy from the primary repository into three arms on that host: rest-server --append-only, rclone serve restic --append-only and restic's native sftp backend. (2) From the backed-up host, attempt restic forget --prune and a direct delete of one pack object: an HTTP DELETE through the REST API on the two server arms, an sftp rm on the sftp arm. Both deletes must be refused on the two append-only arms. (3) Treat the GitHub account as unavailable. Restore the selected application state into an empty target on the destination host, using a second key from restic key add whose password was delivered offline. It passes when restic check --read-data is clean and the state-recovery integrity checks (SQLite integrity, table counts, FTS) match. rest-server is preferred only if it equals rclone on (2) and (3) with fewer moving parts. If deletion protection is not required, sftp plus restic-native custody keeps it out.

Its 'Why use Rest Server?' section says: 'One important safety feature that Rest Server adds is the optional ability to run in append-only mode. proposed.demonstrated_gap: None. The fp-check verdict on the claim 'SOPS closes gap 5' is FALSE POSITIVE. SOPS encrypts a file (for example the restic password), but it puts no backup ciphertext anywhere independent of the GitHub account. By default it decrypts 'if any of the master keys is available', which duplicates restic's native multiple keys. Its key groups use Shamir's Secret Sharing and by default require 'one master key from each of the three groups' to decrypt. That trades recoverability for resistance to compromise, which is the opposite of lost-password recovery. It would also add a second key-custody surface.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Two things together would overturn this. First, a written custody requirement that restic's multiple independent keys cannot meet (for example, no single custodian may unlock the backup: k-of-n). Second, a restore drill with the GitHub account unavailable, in which the restic password is recovered from SOPS key groups and then restic check --read-data and the application-state integrity checks pass on the destination host.
evidence: https://github.com/getsops/docs/blob/main/content/en/docs/usage/identities/key-groups/_index.md : line 10 says that by default the file decrypts 'if any of the master keys is available'. Lines 16-19 say 'keys from multiple groups are required to decrypt a file. SOPS uses Shamir's Secret Sharing to split the data key ... a configurable number of fragments (threshold) are needed'. Lines 27-30 say 'By default, the threshold is set to the number of key groups ... one master key from each of the three groups will be required to decrypt the file.'

https://restic.readthedocs.io/en/stable/070_encryption.html : 'The key command allows you to set multiple access keys or passwords per repository.' This native any-key model already covers lost-password recovery.

Their standing rests on that evidence plus incumbency, not on production-measured restores. It is provisional, not a measured best.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: The WSL2 workstation's Windows-side system dependencies have no declarative reproduction or drift check. This is the layer's overturn_when case: a system dependency that the selected recipes cannot handle. The in-distro recipe (bootstrap-linux.sh) cannot install or check WSL itself, yet adoption/platforms/linux-wsl2.md relies on behavior specific to WSL 2.7.14 (lines 146-149 cite WslClient.cpp at 2.7.14). At origin/main b2767df2, 'winget' occurs in only 2 files, both sdk-runtime-coverage artifacts. Neither winner (restic, uv) covers the Windows host. A WinGet Configuration file is declarative YAML applied through WinGet and PowerShell DSC resources. `winget configure test -f <file>` checks the system against the desired state. `validate` and `export --package-id` exist. The WinGetPackage DSC resource has Id, Source, Version and UseLatest properties, so a WSL version pin can be declared. A Brewfile `winget` entry documents only id: and source:, so brew bundle cannot carry that pin. Trial inputs checked: the package id Microsoft.WSL exists in winget-pkgs, but its version directories stop at 2.7.13. 2.7.14 was absent on 2026-09-29, so WinGet cannot currently apply the recipe's WSL pin. Supply-chain risk to measure: configure downloads PowerShell DSC modules (default %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WinGet\Configuration\Modules), and Microsoft says to check a configuration file's trustworthiness. That is unpinned third-party code unless module versions are pinned.

Declare Microsoft.WSL at the recipe's 2.7.14, Windows Terminal, and a pinned Microsoft.WinGet.DSC module version. Run `winget configure validate` and `winget configure test --disable-interactivity` read-only on the workstation and compare each resource's result with `wsl --version`. As a negative control, declare a mismatching version and require `test` to report non-conformance. Drop to keep_but_compare if any of these holds: `test` cannot evaluate a Version that is absent from the winget source (2.7.14 today); the DSC modules cannot be pinned; or the unattended path needs elevation or an interactive agreement. Applying Microsoft.WSL from inside a WSL session is expected to restart WSL and kill the run (not verified this round), so any apply step must run from the Windows side. Applying the file on a clean Windows install remains an untested boundary until a spare Windows host exists.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Refuted by the requirement ('without copying authentication stores'). `wsl --export` exports a snapshot of the whole distribution. The docs list only `--vhd` and FileName `-` (stdout). The 2.7.14 source (WslClient.cpp ExportDistribution, lines 227-303) accepts only the distro name, a file path or `-`, `--vhd`, and `--format tar|tar.gz|tar.xz|vhd`. It passes only the distro id, the file handle and the format flags to the service, with no include, exclude or path selection. This host keeps file-based authentication stores inside the distro, for example gh's ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, which `gh auth status` reported, so any export copies them. The only way to exclude them is to pipe the tar stream through a denylist filter, which fails open for any store not listed and still streams the bytes out of the distro. A VHD cannot be filtered at all. Whole-image import also restores machine-specific sign-ins and client configuration, instead of reproducing selected tools on an explicitly adopted host. The fp-check review of this refutation found it holds.

It would also need a test that seeds canary files at every auth-store path docs/secret-storage.md defines, exports, and finds none of them in the archive, while the restored selected tools and application state pass the existing restore acceptance on the adopted host.

On an independent empty host, run `backup-fetch LATEST` with restore_command set to `wal-g wal-fetch` and a recovery_target_time. Measure restore time, the last committed row recovered against the target, `wal-verify` status and cleanup. Compare with pg_dump|restic --stdin-from-command + pg_restore, native pg_basebackup plus archive_command, Barman and pgBackRest on the same fixture. Repeat on an M5 Pro through the Homebrew formula.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: The same PITR/RPO requirement is missing as for WAL-G, and the native pg_dump + restic --stdin-from-command baseline closes the independent-restore gap today. Barman's model is a dedicated Barman host that pulls streaming backups and WAL from one or more PostgreSQL servers, with barman-cloud for S3, Azure and GCS (thebuild). 3.20.0 requires Python 3.12 or later. The 3.20.0 release fixed a failure 'restoring an incremental backup from the cloud on a new Barman instance, which is not the same that originally took the backup' (a pg_combinebackup error). Independent-instance restore of incrementals was therefore broken until 2026-08-27, so any adoption has to measure restore on a fresh instance. A multi-server pull model would fit only if the WSL PostgreSQL and the Macs' Apple Container PostgreSQL needed one backup host, and no current recipe requires that. Maintenance: the default branch REL_3_X_master has 107 commits since 2026-07-01, the latest on 2026-08-27. That is lower recent activity than WAL-G but not stale. The supply-chain collector (collect.py on barman==3.20.0) found no known advisory, not yanked, repository not archived, and no security policy published. Publisher concentration could not be assessed because PyPI publishes no upload ACL. License GPL-3.0 (information only).
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Same trigger as WAL-G: a stated RPO, a PITR need or a restore-time bound. Run Barman on the WSL host as the dedicated backup server, with streaming backup and WAL archiving of the fixture. Restore to an independent host at a target time with `barman restore`; its remote-restore options were not verified this round. Separately, restore an incremental backup on a newly installed Barman instance, the path of the 3.20.0 regression. Measure restore time, recovered RPO, `barman check`/verification output and cleanup against WAL-G, pgBackRest and pg_dump|restic. Barman wins only if it matches restore correctness and adds a multi-server pull model that a project needs.

proposed.demonstrated_gap:
Open gap #1: the privacy filter rests on one synthetic canary over tested fields, not arbitrary-content DLP, and no script re-runs it. The collector's redaction processor only allow-lists keys (fail-closed) and matches regex blocked_values. Its stability is alpha for logs and metrics and beta for traces. Yet arbitrary content does reach the pipeline under default settings. Codex's codex.tool_result event carries an 'output snippet', and Claude Code includes user.email under OAuth. Presidio is the maintained open-source detector for such content: NER plus pattern recognizers, run locally. No maintained collector processor wraps it (only a research prototype that calls a PII service over gRPC). Its fit here is therefore a re-runnable post-hoc scanner over what Loki and the SDK spool actually stored. That scanner would also close the 'no script re-runs the canary' half of the gap.
Supply chain: ownership moved from Microsoft to the community-governed Data Privacy Stack org. Microsoft supports the move, the license stays MIT, new images publish to GHCR, and microsoft/presidio now redirects. Pin the new org.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Plant a labelled corpus (synthetic emails, names, API-key and secret shapes, file paths) in prompts, tool outputs and span/log attributes of one real task. Run it through the current collector config. Scan the stored Loki and spool output twice: with presidio-analyzer 2.2.364, and with the redaction processor's regex set alone. Adopt Presidio as the verification scanner if it finds planted values the collector let through, at a false-positive rate the operator accepts. Drop it if the regex set alone reaches the same recall on the planted corpus.

NATIVE GAP CLOSURES (no new repo needed; code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage fetched 2026-09-29)
- Open gap #4 (task attribution) closes by configuration:
  - session.id is on all metrics and events (OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID, default true).
  - prompt.id links every event of one prompt.
  - OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES keys, such as a task id, are added to all metrics and events.
  - claude -p and Agent SDK interaction spans join the caller's trace when TRACEPARENT is set.
- Collector-side spooling: the exporterhelper persistent queue is an in-winner mechanism for gap #5-type loss and recovery acceptance. It uses sending_queue.storage with the file_storage extension, is bounded by queue_size, drops data when full, and recovers after a kill (https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/exporter/exporterhelper/README.md). Whether the SDK receipt lane can export OTLP into it is unverified.

PRIVACY FACTS FOR THE FILTER
- Claude Code puts user.email in telemetry attributes under OAuth. The docs say to filter or redact it in the backend.
- Content-bearing span attributes appear only under detailed beta tracing (ENABLE_BETA_TRACING_DETAILED) and behind the OTEL_LOG_* gates. The attributes are new_context, system_prompt_preview, user_system_prompt, tool_input and response.model_output.
- Under detailed tracing, OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS also releases tool results through new_context.
- With tracing on, each direct Anthropic API request carries a W3C traceparent header. Trace context reaches Anthropic; content does not.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: No engine is qualified for this layer's optional model route on macos-arm64. Every winner is 'untested' there, and the frozen local-inference plan runs only llama.cpp b11146 on the WSL RTX 4090. mlx-lm is Apple's maintained LLM layer on MLX. MLX drives the M5 GPU Neural Accelerators through Metal 4 TensorOps and Metal Performance Primitives. Apple reports M5 time to first token (TTFT) 3.33-4.06x faster than M4 with mlx_lm at a 4096-token prompt, and says the accelerators need macOS 26.2+. The Apple Silicon ecosystem is converging on MLX: Ollama rebuilt its Apple engine on MLX (0.19: 1810 vs 1154 prefill and 112 vs 58 decode tok/s against its GGML Q4_K_M 0.18 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, though the quantizations differ), and vllm-metal and exo both run on MLX/mlx_lm. A July 2026 M5 Pro paper calls MLX 'the stronger prefill baseline on Apple Silicon' compared with llama.cpp. The frozen workload is prefill-heavy (long per-filing prompts, and ttft_ms is a scored metric). The model family is covered: qwen3_5.py (with qwen3_5_moe and qwen3_next) exists at v0.31.3 and on main, and vllm-metal reports mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-8bit. The trial must settle one counterpoint: llama.cpp b11057 already contains PR 27461 (Metal 4 tensor API on M5+, merged 2026-09-01), so using the Neural Accelerators is not unique to MLX, and the paper's llama.cpp baseline predates that fix. Maintenance: 118 default-branch commits since 2026-07-01 (newest 94cdcae13b26 on 2026-09-29), but no tag or release after v0.31.3 (2026-04-22). The repository already hash-locks mlx-lm==0.31.3 with mlx==0.32.2 for its macos-15 CI smoke.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Run on the 64 GB M5 Pro, with macOS 26.2+ as a precondition and the OS build recorded. Use the frozen local-inference workload (same filings, prompts and scoring) and compare the mlx-lm server with llama-server b11146 on Metal: Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit MLX against the C0 UD-Q4_K_M GGUF. On the 24 GB Mac, run the 9B arm instead (MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B, 8-bit MLX against Q8_0 GGUF). The first step is a load check of Qwen3.8 on the locked 0.31.3, falling back to a pin of main commit 94cdcae13b26. Measure TTFT and decode tok/s client-side from streamed responses, the same way for every arm including the llama.cpp control, because the frozen timings.prompt_ms and timings.predicted_per_second fields exist only in llama-server. Also measure micro/macro F1, JSON-valid rate, cold load and peak unified memory. mlx-lm replaces llama.cpp for the Mac route only if F1 and JSON validity are not lower beyond run-to-run noise and TTFT or decode is materially better. Otherwise llama.cpp stays the single engine on both platforms. vllm-metal is a separate data point, because it owns its own paged attention and M5 NAX prefill kernels, so this result does not bound it.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Prefill (TTFT) on the M5 Pro Macs for a prefill-heavy workload. A vendor-authored paper (arXiv 2607.19438v1, Base Compute, July 2026) measured on an Apple M5 Pro with 48 GB. Using hand-written Metal 4 tensor-core kernels, it reports up to 6.4x the prefill throughput of llama.cpp and 3.9x that of MLX. Decode runs 1.02-1.75x over llama.cpp and 1.02-1.33x over MLX, but 0.98x of MLX on Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B. Coverage spans the Qwen3, Qwen3.5/3.6, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 4 families up to 35B. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible 'basert serve' and converts local GGUF, HF or MLX checkpoints to its .base format, so the frozen workload can drive it with the same source weights. Caveats that make a native trial necessary, not a rejection: (1) the only evidence is vendor-authored; (2) the llama.cpp baseline predates llama.cpp PR 27461 (Metal 4 tensor API, merged 2026-09-01); (3) Qwen3.8 support is unverified; (4) the engine's behaviour and telemetry cannot be audited from source against the privacy-filtered requirement, so they are unknown, not refuted; (5) the documented install is a vendor 'curl | sh', while the README says the engine binary is distributed via GitHub Releases, so v0.2.6 can be pinned. proposed.demonstrated_gap: No gap, because the pinned llama-server already serves several models natively. Router mode (launched without a model) provides --models-dir, a --models-preset INI, --models-max (default 4), --models-autoload, and POST /models/load and /models/unload. --sleep-idle-seconds unloads the model and its KV cache after idleness and reloads it on the next task. Both appear in tools/server/README.md at b11146 (the frozen plan's build) and at b11057 (the layer pin), and the v0.5.0 notes (2026-09-23) cite 'more robust server/router operation'. What llama-swap adds beyond this is swapping non-llama.cpp servers: its README says it 'works with any OpenAI and Anthropic API compatible server' and lists vllm. The only GPU co-tenant that makes C1 and C2 resource_infeasible is the vLLM 0.30.0 embeddings service (3,930 MiB), which the frozen plan says is 'Never touched by a window'. Swapping it out would take the memory lane's embeddings offline, and swapping between llama.cpp models adds no capacity that router mode lacks. Upstream is healthy: 123 default-branch commits since 2026-07-01 and v260 on 2026-09-26.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Either of two conditions reopens it. First, the embeddings service is approved for on-demand eviction, or a second non-llama.cpp engine joins the route. Then compare a llama-swap group that exchanges the vLLM embeddings service with llama-server C1 against a systemd-scheduled window, measuring C1 admission, reload latency and embedding-lane errors during the swap. Second, llama-server router mode fails a documented multi-model need (per-model argv, idle TTL) that llama-swap passes on the same host.

- llama.cpp, the conditional route engine (verified here):
  - v0.5.0 (2026-09-23) is the latest non-prerelease. Build tags continue to b11256 (2026-09-29).

- Input-listed component drift (not re-verified): huggingface_hub 1.32.0 against 2.0.0 (a major release, 2026-09-24), and agentsview 0.43.0 against 0.44.0.

ASSESSED BUT NOT PROPOSED (6-proposal cap)
- EricLBuehler/mistral.rs would be keep_but_compare.
  - Maintained: 90 default-branch commits since 2026-07-01, newest 2026-09-25; v0.9.4 (2026-09-24); MIT.
  - The goal 'one engine for CUDA and Metal' is already met by llama.cpp, with CUDA on WSL and Metal with the M5 tensor API since PR 27461.
  - Its only comparison with llama.cpp is self-reported in the README at 2370966: v0.8.2 UQFF q8 against GGUF Q8_0 on GB10, B200 and H100 with Gemma 4 models. It shows roughly 1.35-2.3x prefill and 1.0-1.24x decode.
  - There are no RTX 4090 or Apple figures, and no benchmark of the GGUF path the frozen files would use. Compare it when a 4090 or M5 measurement on the qwen35 GGUF appears.
- grafana/pyroscope: not adopted.
  - No requirement text or open gap asks for CPU profiles. The frozen workload scores server timings and nvidia-smi samples.
  - Adopting it would add a new backend and a new capture agent.
  - If profiles become required, compare open-telemetry/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler first: 267 default-branch commits since 2026-07-01, newest 2026-09-28, no GitHub releases. Its Collector integration was not verified in this round.
  - Pyroscope itself is maintained: 182 commits since 2026-07-01; v2.3.1 (2026-09-08); AGPL-3.0, information only.

VLLM-METAL (round 1, not re-proposed)
- Its README says upstream vLLM supplies the server and scheduler, and mlx_lm supplies the model layers.
- vllm-metal itself owns the paged varlen attention kernel, M5 NAX prefill and speculative decoding. The mlx-lm trial result therefore does not bound it; treat it as a separate data point.
- It reports mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-8bit running on one Mac (2026/08). Latest release v0.30.0 (2026-09-23).

STAR CANDIDATES
- magnitudedev/magnitude: unassessed, not rejected. Created 2026-06-12; 5,458 stars; CLI 0.1.5 (2026-09-23), 0.2.0-alpha on 2026-09-29. No primary evidence on its engine or its fit for the workload was read.

- kvcache-ai/ktransformers: excluded per the brief (fit-judged under agents-models-workers on 2026-09-26).

UNVERIFIED (pending, not refuted)
- M5 Pro Thunderbolt 5 and RDMA support.
- The Macs' macOS versions (Neural Accelerator use needs 26.2+).
- Whether Qwen3.8 loads on mlx-lm 0.31.3, on BaseRT and on TensorRT-LLM.
- TensorRT-LLM on the GeForce RTX 4090 and under WSL2.
- Whether OBI's TLS uprobes attach to Claude Code's native binary.

METHOD
- Maintenance was established with the REST commits?since=2026-07-01 probe on each default branch. No candidate is archived. None is under 90 days old: BaseRT was created 2026-06-26, 95 days ago.
- supply-chain-risk-auditor: only its interpretive rules were applied. Its collector was not run, for two reasons: the targets are upstream repositories rather than a project with manifests, and its per-dependency gh calls exceed the remaining budget.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Lifecycle half of the bridge verb, re-anchored on sources read at v0.14.1. The layer's open gaps list mcporter's persistence, restart, cleanup and recovery stages as not_established (saturation-audit.json lines 5023-5042). The only retained recovery (restart-receipt.json, 2026-09-19, on 0.13.x) was manual. The 2026-09-26 survival quoted docs/daemon.md saying stale metadata 'blocks automatic replacement', but that wording is absent from docs/daemon.md at v0.14.1. Version 0.14.x documents automatic daemon launch (L28) and a reconnect after a definitive transport close (L36). Documented contrasts remain. On a failed call, mcporter returns protocol errors, daemon-generation changes and expired handles to the caller, and ordinary clients never request a shared-server restart (L34). A live or unverified legacy owner blocks startup, an interrupted retirement leaves a marker that blocks startup until migration is rerun, and unverified ownership is resolved manually (L62, L74). The host is one shared per-user daemon, isolated only through MCPORTER_DAEMON_DIR (L86). mcpc 0.7.0 runs a separate bridge process per session with explicit states: live, connecting, reconnecting, disconnected, crashed, unauthorized and expired. It documents background auto-reconnect after network failures or the bridge's own crash (10 s cooldown), restart, close, clean and clean all, and cleanup of orphaned processes, so each session is an owned, disposable unit. Both speak 2026-07-28: mcporter since 0.13.0 (CHANGELOG L222), mcpc since 0.6.0. A web search found no measured comparison of the two, only feature write-ups.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Credential-free fault matrix on linux-wsl2-x86_64 and one macos-arm64 host. The same stdio server and one loopback HTTP server are driven through mcporter 0.14.1 (owned MCPORTER_DAEMON_DIR, throwaway HOME/XDG) and through mcpc 0.7.0 (isolated state directory). Injected faults: SIGKILL of the bridge or host, SIGKILL of the stdio child, stop and start of the HTTP server, explicit restart, cleanup after a crash. Recorded per fault: time to the next successful call, whether a manual step was needed, lost or replayed calls, orphaned processes, residual state files, call parity and warm-call latency. mcpc takes the lifecycle role only if it recovers without a manual step where mcporter needs one, or leaves no orphans where mcporter does, at equal call parity. If mcporter 0.14.1 matches it, the run becomes mcporter's first measured lifecycle evidence and mcpc is dropped.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: On macOS, the only keychain-backed way to run a command with a stored key is the operator's own 'secret' helper. docs/secret-storage.md (lines 566-576) calls it 'the operator's own tool, not part of this repository'; it has no upstream pin, and its Tavily use 'has not been run on a Mac'. Its other documented consumer, the Alpaca paper lane, is a trading gate outside this layer, so the foundation gap is narrow and the path is optional. fnox is an upstream-maintained equivalent. Its OS-keychain provider keeps the value in the macOS Keychain and only the entry name in config. A global ~/.config/fnox/config.toml is always loaded, so nothing has to sit in the checkout; this answers the project-relative-storage objection that refuted secretspec on 2026-09-26. Setting env='exec' keeps secrets out of the interactive shell that AI agents inherit. Limits: 'fnox exec [--replace] [COMMAND]...' has no per-secret selection, so matching the least privilege of 'secret run NAME -- cmd' depends on profiles. On Linux the keychain provider needs a D-Bus Secret Service, which the repository records as absent on WSL2 (a 2026-09-24 decision cited by the 2026-09-26 vote, not re-read), so WSL2 stays on the 0600 store. fnox's own docs say env='exec' limits only ambient exposure and needs OS sandboxing for a hard boundary.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: On a macos-arm64 host, compare fnox v1.36.0 (keychain provider, global config, env='exec', one profile per consumer) with the operator's 'secret run' and with secretspec's keyring provider. Promote fnox to a targeted trial when a foundation key must run through the Keychain on the Macs and it passes with no least-privilege regression. It stays unadopted if profiles cannot confine injection to the named secrets, or if secretspec matches it with less surface.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: The 2026-09-26 sweep refuted gh-stack because the proposal showed 'no current dependent-PR requirement or demonstrated failure of the existing workflow' (GPT-6 fit refuter; the Claude refuter held it as keep_but_compare). This repository's own history supplies that failure. PR #353, opened against #350's head branch and titled 'stacked on #350', was CLOSED unmerged at 2026-09-26T16:57:38Z, two seconds after #350 was squash-merged into main at 16:57:36Z (GitHub GraphQL). The operator's recorded PR-practice notes attribute the closure to merging #350 with `--delete-branch`. They add that merging main into the stacked branch afterwards re-inserted a pre-fix method after the fixed one, which would have silently disabled the fix. The current practice is to avoid stacking. The GitHub branch-management page fetched on 2026-09-29 does not document retargeting of dependent pull requests when a merged head branch is deleted; it says to merge or close an associated open pull request before deleting its branch. GitHub's native stacks do document it: when part of a stack merges, 'the pull requests above stay open and automatically re-target the stack's base branch', and 'the remaining branches are automatically rebased so the next pull request targets the default base branch'. Squash is supported, and every pull request is evaluated against the stack base's rules. gh-stack's `rebase` 'automatically switches to --onto mode' for merged pull requests, and `gh stack merge` is all-or-nothing. gh core has no stack commands. Risks to measure: the feature is public preview and 'subject to change'; v0.1.1 ships binaries with no checksum file; `gh stack init` enables git rerere, whose resolutions live in the common git dir that every owned worktree shares; and API merges of stacks need GitHub's asynchronous merge API. Not addressed by gh-stack: this repository's other stacking failure (#377, a commit-ancestry stack on a main base, 2026-09-27) was a conflict in the hot file manifests/evidence.json, which a cascading rebase will also stop on.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Use a scratch repository with the existing gh sign-in, squash merges, automatic head-branch deletion and a pull_request workflow without a branch filter. Replay the #350/#353 sequence in three arms: (a) plain gh with `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch`, the recorded command; (b) plain gh with `gh pr merge --squash` only, leaving deletion to the repository setting; (c) `gh stack submit`, then `gh stack merge`, or a partial merge followed by `gh stack rebase` and `gh stack push`. Add a hot-file arm in which both layers edit the same JSON registry, as manifests/evidence.json does here. Record for each arm: the upper pull request's state after the lower merge (closed or retargeted), whether its CI runs on the new base, any duplicated hunk or re-inserted definition (diff-of-diffs against the reviewed head), manual commands, conflict stops, and whether rerere writes into the shared common git dir. Adopt gh-stack for stacked work only if (c) keeps the upper pull request open and retargeted with a clean diff where (a) fails. If (b) already avoids the closure and a scripted `git rebase --onto` removes the duplicate-hunk risk, the gap is a practice fix and gh-stack drops to keep_but_compare.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: No gh pull-request create, review or merge result is recorded for this layer, so review automation is unestablished for every candidate. gh's `gh pr review` offers only --approve, --comment and --request-changes with a body. Line-anchored, multi-comment reviews need hand-built JSON through `gh api` on the reviews endpoint. GitHub's official MCP server exposes them as typed tools: `add_comment_to_pending_review` (path, line, side, startLine, subjectType) and `pull_request_review_write` (create, submit, delete and thread resolution), plus create and merge tools, with `--toolsets` scoping and a `--read-only` mode. This is a credible structured alternative, not a demonstrated improvement. It adds tool-schema context to every session that loads it, and it needs a personal access token for the local server or an OAuth sign-in for the remote one. Claude Code's bundled `/code-review --comment` already posts findings as inline PR comments.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: On a scratch pull request, post the same N line-anchored findings (single-line, multi-line, LEFT and RIGHT side) three ways: (a) `gh api` POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/reviews with a comments array; (b) Claude Code `/code-review --comment`; (c) github-mcp-server restricted to `--toolsets pull_requests`. Measure placement accuracy against the diff, failed calls, round trips, and complete tokens including loaded tool schemas. The MCP server earns a role only if (c) places more comments correctly at equal or lower total tokens than (a) and (b), without widening credential exposure beyond the existing gh sign-in.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Worth testing as a complement to difftastic for machine-readable review context: upstream documents entity-level JSON diffs, rename detection and cross-file dependency queries. These provide a concrete way to test whether native reviewers can consume less context without missing consequential changes. The September release also changes handling of added/deleted containers and TypeScript fields. Superiority remains unmeasured, and default-branch maintenance and repository age are unknown because the API was inaccessible.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Compare v0.25.0 at 4cfe1374f796 with difftastic 0.71.0 on at least 30 retained Python, Rust and TypeScript diffs, including moves, renames, formatting-only changes and container deletion. Hold the native reviewer, model and effort constant. Measure changed-entity precision/recall, review defect recall, input tokens and p95 latency on both host profiles. Adopt as a complement only if it reduces reviewer input tokens by at least 20% without reducing defect recall or omitting critical changed entities. Confirm documented features at the release pin: the fetched default-branch README is ahead of that release.
evidence: [Current upstream README](https://github.com/Ataraxy-Labs/sem#sem-diff) documents entity-level diffs, rename detection and JSON/Markdown output; its impact and graph commands expose dependency information.

The fetched release page reports 20 subsequent commits to main; this does not substitute for the required maintenance API check.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Provides a concrete alternative for the layer's unqualified concurrent-agent lifecycle: one tool manages Git worktrees, matching terminal sessions, agent status, review views and cleanup. Worktrunk already documents worktree lifecycle hooks and review previews, so the potential improvement is measurable session ownership and interruption recovery, not basic worktree creation. Upstream documents macOS/Linux installation, but neither exact host profile was tested. Maintenance and repository age remain unknown.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: Compare v0.1.268 at 1d5e7da97bb3 with the qualified Worktrunk plus gh baseline. Run 20 matched trials per host with three concurrent native-agent worktrees, interrupted agents, merge conflicts and cancelled tasks. Measure manual recovery actions, completion time, orphaned sessions/worktrees and correct branch/diff association. Workmux would earn adoption only with zero lost changes or cross-worktree writes, complete cleanup and at least 25% fewer manual recovery actions. Keep gh responsible for GitHub PR operations in both arms.
evidence: [Upstream features](https://github.com/raine/workmux#features) document coupled worktree/terminal creation, agent monitoring, review and lifecycle cleanup.

[Agent status tracking](https://github.com/raine/workmux#agent-status-tracking) lists Claude Code and Codex support. [Dashboard documentation](https://github.com/raine/workmux#workmux-dashboard) describes separate working-change and branch-review diff views.

[Installation](https://github.com/raine/workmux#installation) documents Homebrew for macOS/Linux and Cargo. [Requirements](https://github.com/raine/workmux#requirements-1) identify Git and tmux or another backend; the repository page identifies the MIT license.

[Release v0.1.268](https://github.com/raine/workmux/releases/tag/v0.1.268), dated 2026-09-26, identifies commit 1d5e7da97bb3. Its release notes link a comparison rather than describing individual changes, so no specific feature is attributed to this release.

[Worktrunk's current README](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk#worktrunk-makes-git-worktrees-as-easy-as-branches) already documents hooks, merge automation and review previews; these overlapping capabilities must remain in the comparison.

proposed.demonstrated_gap: Offers explicit structural-risk ordering and logical change groups as inputs to native code review, extending the comparison beyond presenting changed syntax. Its documented benchmark measures triage characteristics across Rust repositories, not defect-detection precision or recall, so it does not establish better review quality than the current bridge or sem. Retain for comparison when risk-prioritized review is required. Creation date, maintenance, release pin and exact platform qualification remain unresolved.
proposed.comparison_that_would_overturn: First compare inspect's deterministic diff/MCP context with sem plus difftastic on retained PRs containing independently labeled defects and dependency changes. Feed each context to the same native-account reviewer, holding model and effort constant; this avoids requiring new provider credentials. Measure critical-defect recall, false-positive findings, grouping accuracy, input tokens and latency on both hosts. Promote only if risk ordering reduces tokens or review time by at least 20% without reducing critical-defect recall. Resolve an immutable source pin and verify the supported build before a native trial.

output.notes:
Coverage is bounded by retrieval failures: all eight search queries returned empty responses. Sixteen public GitHub API URL fetches returned HTTP 403; three additional API URL attempts failed because the web channel did not support open. Counts include failed attempts and delegated queries and count individual queries/URLs rather than batch invocations. The eight-page fetch budget was exhausted. Required default-branch activity since 2026-07-01 and repository creation dates therefore remain unknown; no repository was excluded for maintenance, and no TOO NEW TO ASSESS classification could be established. Null metadata means unknown, not absent. No installations, shell commands, candidate execution or credential access occurred. Skills were applied to discovery, claim verification and uncertainty handling; no complete dependency or vulnerability audit was performed.

Winner observations: [gh v2.101.0](https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.101.0) was released on 2026-09-15 at 0cf1092493af. Its fixes include remote-branch deletion with owner-case mismatch, a useful fixture for the outstanding lifecycle qualification. This release evidence does not establish successful PR creation, review or merge on these hosts. Given the supplied evidence gaps, gh's winner standing for PR operations remains incumbent and provisional rather than a measured best. [Difftastic 0.71.0](https://github.com/Wilfred/difftastic/releases/tag/0.71.0), released 2026-09-18 at b7d119e90ac9, matches the supplied pin. Worktrunk and difftastic have supplied historical evidence, but this read-only sweep adds neither host recertification nor a matched superiority result. The supplied Worktrunk v0.80.0 drift and codex-for-claude v1.0.6 status could not be independently refreshed because their [Worktrunk release API](https://api.github.com/repos/max-sixty/worktrunk/releases/latest) and [bridge release API](https://api.github.com/repos/openai/codex-plugin-cc/releases/latest) failed. No archival, ownership or license change was verified; unavailable metadata does not clear those checks. No model-quality claim was made. No seeded repositories were supplied. Previous refutations were not treated as current evidence, and no new rejection is asserted without primary support.
